newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zairean rebels tighten grip on southeastern town.
newsitem.headline: Zairean rebels tighten grip on southeastern town.

text.p: Zairean rebels reportedly tightened their grip on a town in southeastern Zaire on Tuesday and Rwanda warned that sending French-speaking African troops to Zaire would complicate the war.
Military sources in the region said rebels had taken total control of the strategic town of Kalemie and were pouring in reinforcements to push further south towards the town of Moba.

The sources, monitoring the war in Africa's second largest country, told Reuters rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL) were pursuing retreating government troops on the way to Moba.
"They are tightening their grip. Kalemie is under total military control and government forces are being pursued on the Moba route," said one source who declined to be identified.
The Zairean government said on Tuesday the Lake Tanganyika port had fallen but added fighting continued elsewhere in the town.
The sources said rebels might try to press on to Lubumbashi, 800 km (500 miles) from Kalemie and Zaire's second largest city and capital of mineral-rich Shaba province bordering on Zambia.
A source reported clashes outside Shabunda town and said rebels were moving very close to Lubutu, where seven km (four miles) to the east are camped some 120,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees.
There are an estimated 35,000 Rwandan refugees at Shabunda, which like Lubutu is near the northern parts of the rebel-held areas.
Rebels were also fighting government troops outside the town of Watsa, which was until its fall last week a centre for mercenaries recruited by Kinshasa for its counter-offensive.
"It's a war being fought on three fronts. It is a strategy to tax the Zairean army and its mercenaries," the source added.

Meanwhile, Emmanuel Ndahiro, chief advisor to Rwanda's Vice-President and military strongman Major-General Paul Kagame, warned that Africa's latest war would not end if Kinshasa brought in troops from French-speaking Chad, Morocco and Togo.
"The involvement of foreign troops in Zaire will only complicate the war in Zaire. What is interesting is that the forces have a common denominator -- French-speaking," he said.
"One cannot avoid speculating these countries have Rwanda in mind (to counter-balance). We also ask: who is paying for these countries because they are poor and all have internal problems?"

Zairean Defence Ministry officials said on Monday troops from Togo, Chad and Morocco were standing by to fly to Zaire and it had invited Israel and China to help train new brigades of up to 26,000 fighters.
Togo on Tuesday denied it planned to send troops to Zaire.
"There are no Togolese troops preparing to leave for Zaire. We haven't even discussed it," Togo's Foreign Minister Pierre Koffi Panou, on a private visit to Paris, told Reuters.
Ndahiro said foreign powers including Belgium were trying to internationalise the conflict in order to justify the deployment of an international military force in Zaire.

"Some people and the Belgians are trying to drag us into a war that is purely an internal Zairean matter. Zaire's counter-offensive has failed so they are seeking an international force to help reverse the rebel advance," he said.
Zaire accuses Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda of backing the ADFL led by Laurent Kabila, whose hometown is Kalemie. All three deny sending in troops to fight alongside the rebels in the east.
Some Ugandan and Rwandan troops crossed into Zaire at the start of the revolt on what they said were "hot pursuit" raids. Journalists who saw them said their role was greater than that.
Belgium said last week it had reports foreign troops, including Rwandans, were in eastern Zaire on the rebel side.
Since October, Kabila's forces have taken over a 1,000-km (600-mile) long strip of eastern Zaire bordering on Uganda, Rwanda, Burundi and Lake Tanganyika facing western Tanzania.
